beats.text: Monday, nineteen hundred. Anna gets up before dawn. Today is wash day. And it will take her the whole day.
One load of laundry needs about fifty gallons of water. Every drop, carried in by hand.
She hauls it from the pump. Heats it on the stove. Scrubs every shirt on a washboard. Boils it. Wrings it. Hangs it out.
In one year, she walks about a hundred and fifty miles, just carrying water. That's thirty-six tons.
But the work isn't over. Tuesday is ironing day. With heavy irons, heated on that same stove.
So every week began the same way. Monday, washing. Tuesday, ironing.
Then came running water. Electricity. And the washing machine.
Today, you press one button. And you don't even have to watch.
Anna's whole day, and thirty-six tons of water. Now it's one button.

sources: One load (washing, boiling, rinsing) about 50 gallons of water; per year a housewife walked about 148 miles toting water and carried over 36 tons. Digital History, University of Houston, 'Private Life', based on Susan Strasser, Never Done: A History of American Housework (1982).
Wash day Monday, ironing Tuesday with sad irons heated on the stove: traditional household routine (Strasser 1982). Anna is illustrative.
Film: Lumière, 'Laveuses sur la rivière' (1897), public domain, illustrative (Internet Archive).
